q: What is the clear span of a beam?
o: The distance between the inner faces of its supports
The distance between the centers of its supports
The total length of the beam including its bearings
The distance between its points of inflection
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Clear span is the open distance you can walk through between supports. Center-to-center span is longer by half a support width at each end.

o: The shortening of a column under axial load
The sideways movement of a member under transverse load
The rotation of a footing under uneven pressure
The stretching of a tie rod under tension
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Deflection is the sag of a beam or slab. It is limited (for example span/360 under live load for floors carrying brittle finishes) so finishes do not crack and floors do not feel bouncy.

q: A simple beam has positive (sagging) moment along its whole length. What shape does it deflect into?
o: Concave downward, hogging along its whole length
An S-shape with a point of inflection
Concave upward, sagging along its whole length
It stays straight
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: The curvature follows the sign of the moment: positive moment gives concave-up curvature. Where the moment diagram changes sign, the deflected shape has a point of inflection.

q: How is the internal shear force at a section of a beam found?
o: As the sum of all the moments taken about the section
As the total load divided by the depth of the beam
As the reaction at the far support only
As the algebraic sum of the transverse forces on one side of the section
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Cut the beam and take one side as a free body: the shear at the cut balances the sum of the vertical loads and reactions on that side.

q: A simply supported beam under uniform load has its span doubled, with the same load per metre and section. By what factor does its midspan deflection grow?
o: 16 times
2 times
4 times
8 times
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: δ = 5wL⁴/384EI, so deflection grows with the fourth power of the span: 2⁴ = 16. That is why long spans are usually governed by deflection rather than strength.

q: What is a haunch on a beam?
o: A notch cut into the beam's end where it sits on the support
A local deepening of the beam near a support to resist higher moment and shear
A thin flange added to the top of the beam at midspan
A hook bent at the end of a main bar
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Near the supports of continuous beams and frames, moments and shears peak. A haunch deepens the beam only there, instead of making the whole beam deeper.

q: What is the span of a structure?
o: The height of a column from floor to floor
The width of slab strip carried by one beam
The distance a member crosses between two supports
The overall depth of a beam from top to bottom
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Span is the horizontal distance a beam, slab or truss must bridge between supports. Longer spans need deeper members.

q: In a fixed or continuous beam, what length acts like the span of an equivalent simple beam?
o: The full clear span
The distance from face to face of the columns plus the beam depth
Twice the clear span
The distance between the points of inflection
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: The segment between the points of zero moment bends like a simply supported beam. In a fixed-ended beam under uniform load these points are about 0.21L from each support.

q: Where is the vertical shear stress greatest in a rectangular beam section?
o: At the neutral axis
At the top face
At the bottom face
It is the same everywhere
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Shear stress τ = VQ/Ib is zero at the top and bottom faces and peaks at the neutral axis, at 1.5 times the average V/A for a rectangle.

o: The axial force that shortens a column
The internal moment that tends to bend a member at a section
The twisting action on a shaft about its axis
The sliding of one part of a joint over another
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Bending moment at a section equals the sum of the moments of all forces on one side of it. It causes tension on one face and compression on the other.

o: The downward sag of a beam under its service load
A sloped top surface given to a roof slab for drainage
A slight upward curve built into a beam to offset its expected deflection
The rotation of a beam end at its support
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: A cambered beam or truss is made curving slightly upward so that under dead load it settles to about level. It is common in long-span steel beams and precast members.

q: A beam's clear span is 5.0 m and it rests on 0.40 m wide columns. What is its center-to-center span?
n: Center-to-center span = clear span + half a column width at each end = 5.0 + 0.2 + 0.2 = 5.4 m.
formula: L(c-c) = clear span + ½ support width at each end
steps: Half of each 0.40 m support = 0.20 m

o: A simple span carried between the cantilevered ends of the adjoining spans
A span hung by cables from a tower, as in a suspension bridge
A beam hung from the floor above by steel rods
A span that has no supports of any kind
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: In a cantilever-and-suspended-span system, the adjoining spans cantilever out and a simple span is pinned between their tips, near where the moment would be zero. It makes a continuous-looking beam statically determinate.

q: What resists the transverse shear force at a section of a beam?
o: The bending stresses at the top and bottom
The vertical shearing stresses across the section
The axial stress in the beam
The bearing stress at the support
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Vertical shearing stresses spread over the cross-section add up to the shear force V. They come with equal horizontal shearing stresses on longitudinal planes.

q: What is the resisting moment of a beam section?
o: The reaction moment at a fixed support
The moment that causes a member to twist about its axis
The internal compression-tension couple that balances the moment
The largest moment shown on the moment diagram
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: The compression force C and tension force T in the section form a couple, C × lever arm, that equals the external bending moment and keeps the section in equilibrium.

q: What is horizontal shearing stress in a beam?
o: The shear at the supports only, where the reactions act
The stress produced by horizontal wind load on the beam
The bearing stress where the beam rests on the column
Shear along horizontal planes that keeps layers from sliding
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: If a beam were a stack of loose planks, the planks would slide past each other when bent. Horizontal shear is what prevents that sliding in a solid beam; it is why glulam glue lines and composite shear studs matter.

o: A rigid member that carries loads across its length to its supports
A vertical member that carries axial load down to the footing
A cable that can carry tension only
A plate that carries load in two directions
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Beams take transverse loads and carry them to supports through bending and shear. Columns carry axial load, cables carry tension only, and slabs spread load in one or two directions.

q: At what point along a beam does the shear diagram cross zero?
o: At the supports only
At the point of maximum bending moment
At the point of maximum deflection in every case
At the point of inflection
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Since dM/dx = V, the moment peaks where the shear is zero. That is why the shear diagram is drawn first when looking for the design moment.

q: How is the change in bending moment between two points of a beam related to the shear diagram?
o: It equals the slope of the shear diagram
It equals the largest shear value
It equals the area of the shear diagram between those points
It is unrelated to the shear diagram
ref: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated; Hibbeler, Structural Analysis; NSCP 2015 Sec. 406.2.3
n: Because dM/dx = V, integrating gives ΔM = area under the shear diagram. Likewise, the change in shear equals the area under the load diagram.
